title: Flock Municipal Cancellations & Non-Renewals Database
subtitle: Cities and agencies that terminated, did not renew, let expire, suspended, or rescinded Flock Safety ALPR contracts
scope_note: Includes municipal/agency actions ending or pausing Flock use. Does not claim a complete national census. Aggregator tallies (e.g. ~82 contracts across 28 states Aug 2021 to May 2026 per SF Standard / Ban Flock Cameras) are larger than this verified dossier. Private/HOA Flock cameras may remain after a city contract ends.

headline_aggregator_claims.sf_standard_ban_flock: 82 contracts terminated across 28 states (Aug 2021 to May 2026); 39 in Jan to May 2026
headline_aggregator_claims.npr_feb_2026: At least ~30 localities deactivated cameras or canceled contracts since early 2025

why_cities_leave: Unauthorized or unexpected federal / out-of-state data access
Vendor trust failures (unauthorized installs, reactivation, misrepresentations)
Public / resident backlash and organized opposition
New state compliance, audit, retention, or liability burden
summary.citation_hygiene: The 64 records_in_dossier each have their own sources. Larger headline counts (for example ~82 contracts) come from secondary tallies such as SF Standard / Ban Flock Cameras. Cite those named sources separately. Do not treat the larger tallies as identical to this 64-record verified list. Rows whose Verification_Status includes Aggregator-aligned still need a primary confirmation before calling them verified. Clear municipal exits (Terminated / Non-renewal / Rescinded / Pre-install cancel) currently number 52; the other 12 rows are pauses, suspensions, expire/renegotiate, or delayed-renewal cases.

data_dictionary.Jurisdiction: City, county, campus, or agency name.
data_dictionary.Action_Type: Terminated | Non-renewal | Expired | Suspended | Rescinded | Pre-install cancel | Paused.

data_dictionary.Spotlight: Y for featured serious cases (Oshkosh, Verona, Staunton).

data_dictionary.Summary: Short narrative of what happened and why.
data_dictionary.Primary_Source_URL: Best primary or strong local/national source.
data_dictionary.Verification_Status: Verified local/primary | Verified major press | Aggregator-aligned (confirm).
data_dictionary.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Private cams remaining, loopholes, bags, delayed removal, possible renegotiation.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Resident council testimony; CEO email conflicted with city values

records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Removal delayed; some cameras still up into Feb 2026 per News Leader.

records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Removal fight after cancel; confirm final hardware status.

records.Primary_Reasons: Vendor misrepresentation (heat maps); Police chief trust failure; Public backlash
records.Summary: Council approved a one-year renewal amid vocal public opposition, then unanimously rescinded within ~24 hours after Police Chief Dean Smith said Flock misrepresented heat-map tracking capability at the council meeting. Cameras powered off and bagged.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Hardware bagged while removal coordinated.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Loss of trust in vendor (not PD); Data-sharing / federal access fears
records.Summary: Common Council voted not to renew; contract lapsed December. Officials and residents framed the decision as lack of public trust in Flock Safety. Cameras remained up for months; city covered them pending physical removal.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Physical removal lagged contract end; interim lens covers.

records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Advocates seeking assurance city will not replace with similar system.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy / constitutional concerns; Outside agency / ICE access fears; Split council
records.Summary: Police chief did not bring renewal to council after finding council deeply split. Council president cited privacy, corporate sharing, ICE access fears, and credited residents and advocacy groups for raising concerns.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Removal at contract expiration end of month.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Sanctuary-city conflict; Third-party disclosure language; Outside agency access concerns
records.Summary: Common Council ended the contract after activist campaign and protests outside city hall. Resolution cited sanctuary policies and documented outside-agency access without explicit local authorization.

records.Primary_Reasons: Out-of-state access; Immigration / sanctuary urgency; Public / grassroots pressure (Get the Flock Out)
records.Summary: Council voted 6-1 to terminate after out-of-state agencies accessed city data. Widely reported as first California city to end a Flock contract; grassroots organizing credited alongside immigration-enforcement urgency.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy / constitutional concerns

records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Private/HOA Flock cameras remain; some pre-Flock city LPR gear unaffected.

records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Suspension pending confidence in safeguards; not necessarily permanent cancel.

records.Summary: LAPD let three-year agreement expire (~138 pole cameras since 2023). Audit/reporting cited federal access and immigration-enforcement risk. Some outlets note possible renegotiation with stricter terms.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: May renegotiate; not necessarily a permanent ban.

records.Summary: Suspended fixed-site Flock program after review found immigration-related search activity against city policy. City covered ~72 cameras with bags; commissioners called for removal pending audit.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Suspension + bags; final removal decision pending audit/commission.

records.Primary_Reasons: Discontinued program; Data sharing disabled; Privacy climate
records.Summary: Discontinued contract; covered lenses and disabled data sharing.

records.Primary_Reasons: Unauthorized federal access; Public backlash; Sanctuary / privacy climate
records.Summary: El Cerrito council voted in May 2026 not to renew after federal agencies accessed data from about 40 cameras without local police knowledge. The contract expired June 6; cameras were supposed to be offline, but residents flagged a unit still flickering. KALW reported July 31, 2026 that police began physically removing cameras; Flock told the city removal would run through about August 18.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Contract expired June 6, 2026 after May non-renewal. KALW reported July 31, 2026 that police began physically removing cameras; Flock told the city removal would run through about August 18. Residents had flagged units still flickering after supposed offline date.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Pause on new ALPR bids until citywide surveillance policy; Physical removal
records.Summary: City Council voted 6-1 on June 16, 2026 to immediately cancel Flock, stop data collection, remove cameras, and delay new ALPR bids until a citywide surveillance policy exists. Staff confirmed all 15 city Flock cameras removed by early July 2026.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Private Flock cameras elsewhere in area not covered by city vote.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Fixed-ALPR policy requiring council approval; Organized opposition (Deflock Harrisonburg)
records.Summary: Harrisonburg City Council voted 4-0 on July 29, 2026 to end the Flock contract and adopt a policy generally prohibiting mounted ALPRs without express council approval. About 31 Falcon cameras; systems to go dark ~July 31 with removal work order.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Broader ban on all future mass-surveillance vendors not passed in same vote.

records.Primary_Reasons: Regional Shenandoah Valley cancel wave; Public backlash
records.Summary: Elkton ended its Flock contract the week before Harrisonburg’s July 29, 2026 cancel, per regional coverage of the Shenandoah Valley exit wave (alongside earlier Staunton / Charlottesville exits).
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Camera count and exact council vote date not detailed in Harrisonburg-focused coverage.

records.Primary_Reasons: Data ownership / local-control concerns; Seeking replacement vendor
records.Summary: Salem Mayor Dominick Pangallo and Police Chief Lucas Miller said the city would not renew Flock and would remove installed ALPRs over insufficient data protections, while seeking systems that better retain local control, a cancel-then-replace risk pattern.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: City indicated intent to replace with another ALPR vendor retaining local data control.

records.Primary_Reasons: Privacy / mass-surveillance concerns; Outside and federal access risk; Physical removal emphasis
records.Summary: Monroe County Commissioners voted to cancel the Flock contract (~6 cameras), citing privacy and mass-surveillance concerns and risk that plate/location data could be accessed by outside or federal agencies. Coverage notes Bloomington also ending its Flock contract; officials emphasized cameras must come down, not only contracts ending. CBS4 Indy / WIBC / WBIW July 28, 2026.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eguU9gQfZ54 (CBS4 Indy). Bloomington city exit tracked separately (CAN-2026-017).

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy concerns; Early buyout of two-year contract
records.Summary: Stoughton City Council unanimously voted July 28, 2026 to terminate Flock after months of resident opposition. Five cameras (four ALPR + one live feed); ~$12,500 remaining buyout on a two-year/$25,000 contract; removal and data deletion directed; commitment not to swap to similar tech without 30 days’ notice and public input. Seventh Dane County entity ending Flock per local reporting.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NtGB6BMvFU (WKOW 27). WKOW video page: https://www.wkow.com/video/stoughton-votes-to-remove-flock-cameras/video_5cb9e98e-a618-5f0b-bff7-71342db8f8c6.html

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy concerns; ACLU of RI advocacy letter; Misuse/federal-access fears
records.Summary: South Kingstown Town Council voted unanimously (5-0) on July 27, 2026 to terminate Flock and remove cameras ASAP after hundreds of resident emails and an ACLU of Rhode Island letter. Contract ~$30,300/year; ~6-7 cameras active since Feb 2026. Seeking partial refund. State Police Flock on state roads may remain nearby.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: YouTube WPRI https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5a4l65Jen3E and WJAR https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9RRqBtry1CU cover the same South Kingstown cancel. ACLU RI: https://www.riaclu.org/news/south-kingstown-cancels-flock-safety-contract-after-community-advocacy-aclu-letter/

records.Primary_Reasons: Vendor trust failure; Unauthorized reactivation without notice; Privacy review
records.Summary: After a May 2026 Select Board order powered down six Flock cameras for policy review, police found on July 30 that Flock had reactivated five of six cameras on public ways without notifying the town. Select Board cut power, ordered contract termination, and directed removal of all six cameras.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Power cut immediately; physical removal ordered for all six public-way units.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Early-exit accepted; Low local crime cited; RI cancel wave
records.Summary: Narragansett Town Council voted unanimously August 3, 2026 to terminate Flock early and accept early-exit penalties. Agreement had been set to run into 2027; about four cameras (one stolen). Came one week after South Kingstown’s cancel. Boston Globe notes ~$12,600 initial / ~$12,000 yearly from forfeiture funds.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: WJAR Aug 4 confirm; GoLocalProv covers RI wave after South Kingstown.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy / nationwide sharing concerns; Contract-language amendment
records.Summary: Oklahoma City Council deferred an August 4, 2026 vote on a ~$270,000 Flock renewal (~90 cameras through June 30, 2027) so staff could amend agreement language. Journal Record says the system had been running without a valid contract since July 1; item expected back about August 18. Not a cancel—a delayed renewal under public pressure.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Cameras reportedly still active pending Aug 18 return; not a termination.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy concerns; First Nebraska municipal reject
records.Summary: Ord City Council voted 5-0 on August 3, 2026 to begin removing two Flock cameras, described as Nebraska’s first outright municipal reject. Cameras were installed under a Valley County / Region 26 emergency-management grant and were still operating after the city vote pending county / Region 26 follow-up (board discussion aimed around Aug. 11).
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: County ownership / Region 26 grant means city vote alone may not power cameras down; removal coordination ongoing as of Aug. 4 reporting.

records.Primary_Reasons: Third-party / network access risk; Campus privacy backlash; Vendor swap
records.Summary: Stanford University announced it ended its Flock Safety agreement and is replacing campus entrance ALPR with Genetec Cloudrunner: short cloud hold, then university-controlled storage with no third-party network access built into the architecture (Palo Alto Online citing Stanford Report, Aug. 4, 2026). Note: swapping vendors is not ending campus ALPR.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Campus ALPR continues under Genetec; Flock exit is a network-isolation choice, not a plate-scanner ban.

records.Primary_Reasons: Fourth Amendment concerns; Sheriff non-renewal; Privacy / mass-surveillance risk
records.Summary: Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple told the Board of Supervisors on August 5, 2026 he will not renew the sheriff’s office Flock Safety contract when it expires at the end of September, citing serious Fourth Amendment concerns about the technology whether or not the county uses every feature. Teeple had defended the cameras at a 2025 town hall. Cities and towns inside the county that run their own Flock programs are not bound by the sheriff’s decision. Decommissioning was expected as the contract lapses.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Sheriff’s office cameras only; municipal Flock programs inside Pinal County may continue. Hardware removal timing after September lapse still TBD. Official PCSO Facebook reel: https://www.facebook.com/reel/3622783047870589

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy / mass-surveillance concerns; Data-sharing concerns
records.Summary: South Tucson City Council voted February 17, 2026 to cancel its Flock Safety contract after months of resident opposition organized in part by Deflock Tucson, making South Tucson the third Arizona city in that reporting wave after Flagstaff and Sedona. Officials later explored alternative surveillance options while police said losing the tool affected investigations.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Council explored replacement surveillance vendors after the Flock exit.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Data ownership / AI training concerns; Vendor swap planned
records.Summary: Sierra Vista City Council directed staff in a February 24, 2026 work session to end the Flock contract (30-day notice); city officials said the agreement was officially terminated April 2, 2026. About 16 grant-funded plate readers had been purchased for police. Residents and Cochise County Supervisor Frank Antenori raised concerns about Flock owning image rights and AI use. Cameras remained mounted but offline pending Flock removal; the city planned to seek another ALPR vendor with the same grant funds.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Hardware still up but not operational pending vendor removal; city shopping replacement ALPR.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Federal access / privacy concerns; Early termination fee
records.Summary: Albany City Council voted 4-2 on May 27–28, 2026 to end its Flock Safety contract after earlier suspending the city’s single active downtown camera in February over federal-access concerns. The camera was stolen after power-down. Formal termination was effective June 29; early exit cost about $7,000 per city manager reporting. Plans for three additional cameras were dropped.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Only one camera had been deployed of four purchased; stolen after February suspension.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Renewal delay; Privacy / ordinance campaign
records.Summary: Chandler City Council delayed a decision on renewing its about $153,000 Flock Safety contract until its August 13, 2026 meeting amid resident opposition organized by East Valley Unite and related advocacy. FOX 10 / AZFamily reporting on the Pinal County non-renewal wave noted Chandler’s delay alongside Flagstaff, Sedona, and South Tucson exits. Not a cancel—a delayed renewal under public pressure.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Cameras still in use pending Aug. 13 renewal vote; not a termination.

records.Primary_Reasons: Officer database / ALPR misuse; Internal audit; Agency integrity response
records.Summary: Sumter County Sheriff Patrick Breeden suspended the Sheriff’s Office use of Flock after an internal audit flagged Detective Brandy Almany’s alleged personal-use searches of Flock ALPR, Florida’s DAVID, and CCIS involving her husband’s ex-wife. Almany was arrested and terminated (July 23, 2026). Breeden ordered a complete internal audit of agency databases while Flock remains suspended.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Temporary suspension pending complete internal audit; agency had not announced when or whether cameras would return as of July 24, 2026 reporting. Related misuse row: FLK-2026-020.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy / surveillance concerns; Regional grant reject
records.Summary: Leon County Commission on July 14, 2026 unanimously stripped about $440,000 in regional public-safety grant funding that would have expanded Flock ALPRs in neighboring Wakulla, Jefferson, Liberty, and Taylor counties (pass-through via Leon County Sheriff’s Office). Commissioners approved other grant items, directed a September workshop on county authority to regulate or ban ALPRs locally, after packed public comment opposing surveillance expansion.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Rejects regional expansion grant funding, not removal of existing Leon County cameras; September 2026 authority/workshop follow-up pending.

records.Primary_Reasons: Data-sharing controversies; Public backlash; Vendor swap (Axon)
records.Summary: After data-sharing controversies, Syracuse Common Council moved to end Flock on city streets and approved a multi-year Axon plate-reader contract. By mid-July 2026, Flock confirmed its 13 city-approved readers were removed from city property. Axon cameras were expected afterward: a vendor swap, not an end to mass plate scanning. Separate university / private Flock installs can remain.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: City property Flock removed; Axon replacement approved. Private / university Flock units may remain. Not a ban on ALPR.

records.Primary_Reasons: Public backlash; Privacy concerns; Vendor swap (Axon)
records.Summary: Grand Chute’s board canceled its Flock contract and signed an Axon camera agreement the same night. Reporting says about 23 cameras stay in place for a swap targeted around September 1: another Flock-to-Axon vendor swap, not an end to plate scanning.
records.Incomplete_Exit_Notes: Flock exit with same-night Axon replacement; cameras remain for swap. Not a ban on ALPR.
